title: Durable regenerative closure of diabetic foot ulcers after ischemia and pressure are treated

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that enables diabetic foot ulcers to close and remain intact after treatment ends, once inadequate blood supply, harmful pressure and infection have been addressed. Its target is the persistent ulcer in an otherwise adequately treated foot: repair that survives the return to ordinary protected loading, rather than closure that depends on continued use of the study product. The supplied evidence establishes the clinical need, but does not demonstrate that this capability has been achieved.

Conceptual synthesis: the regenerative ambition extends beyond covering the wound to restoring functional tissue. Load-bearing strength and resistance to infection are proposed properties that would require direct assessment; complete closure and fewer subsequent ulcers would not, by themselves, establish either property or prove regeneration. The concept concerns local repair in diabetic skin and does not imply correction of diabetes, neuropathy or every cause of chronic ulceration.

significance.text: Armstrong, Tan, Boulton and Bus's 2023 JAMA review estimates that diabetic foot ulcers affect approximately 18.6 million people worldwide annually, including 1.6 million in the United States. These ulcers precede about 80% of lower-extremity amputations among people with diabetes and are associated with approximately 30% five-year mortality. These figures establish the seriousness and scale of the problem; they do not establish how many patients would qualify for this proposed treatment or what fraction of amputations it could prevent.

The potentially revolutionary advance would be sustained repair in ulcers that remain stalled despite appropriate underlying care. Its direct consequence would be durable closure of the treated wounds. Reducing ulcer-related amputation risk is a plausible downstream benefit because ulcers can progress to infection, gangrene and limb loss, but that benefit and its magnitude would require measurement. The associated mortality burden does not establish that restoring skin repair would improve survival.

The impact has important boundaries. Local repair would not itself restore protective sensation, correct persistent ischemia, remove venous hypertension or eliminate harmful mechanical exposure. Footwear, preventive care and management of vascular disease would remain relevant after closure. Subsequent ulcers can arise elsewhere, including on the opposite foot, so successful repair at one site would not necessarily prevent all future foot ulcers.

Evaluative synthesis: within this concept, faster initial healing without improved durability would be an incremental advance rather than completion of the proposed breakthrough. Acute traumatic-wound healing offers a possible benchmark for functional repair, but differences in sensation, circulation, metabolic disease and loading prevent a simple equivalence. No supplied historical breakthrough comparison establishes a stronger analogy.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved target is reliable, lasting repair in diabetic ulcers that persist after adequate perfusion, effective offloading and infection control. The scientific challenge is to identify and correct the residual barriers to repair without assuming that every persistent wound has one underlying repair-program defect. The supplied reviews support impaired healing and prior testing of individual topical growth factors; they do not establish a single mechanism whose correction would produce durable regeneration.

A major interpretive barrier is separating failure of repaired tissue from renewed injury or ulceration elsewhere. The 2023 review reports one cohort in which only 17% of recurrences occurred at the identical location and 48% occurred on the contralateral foot. Those findings do not disprove intrinsic repair defects, but they prevent patient-level recurrence from serving as a direct measure of the durability of the original repair.

Engineering synthesis: a successful intervention would need to produce tissue that remains functional after product withdrawal and renewed protected loading. Concrete development barriers include measuring mechanical integrity beyond visible closure, demonstrating any claimed restoration of tissue structure, and assessing infection resistance separately from baseline infection control. Treatment effects must also be distinguishable from differences in offloading, footwear and preventive care. The supplied evidence does not identify a validated intervention that meets this entire specification.

current_state.text: The JAMA review published on July 3, 2023, with a literature search through May 2023, reports approximately 30–40% healing at 12 weeks and 23% of patients having a nonhealed ulcer at 12 months. It reports recurrence estimates of 42% at one year, 58% at three years and 65% at five years. These are historical population estimates drawn from different datasets, not a common treatment-specific trajectory or a demonstrated ceiling on therapeutic performance. Patient-level recurrence also includes new ulcers away from the original wound.

Approximately half of people with a diabetic foot ulcer have lower-extremity peripheral artery disease, according to the same review. First-line management includes debridement, reducing weight-bearing pressure on the ulcer, treating infection and addressing ischemia, including revascularization when indicated. The review also summarizes short-term healing benefits for placenta-derived products and negative-pressure wound therapy. These findings document useful existing care without establishing the proposed combination of regeneration and long-term treated-site durability.

Tian and colleagues' network meta-analysis, published on June 25, 2025, searched through January 12, 2025. It reports improved healing rates with epidermal growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor and platelet-rich plasma compared with standard care. The review also identifies generally low methodological quality and inconsistent outcome timing. Its outcomes do not include long-term recurrence, so the reported healing benefits and treatment rankings cannot establish durable regeneration or show whether historical recurrence rates improve, remain unchanged or worsen.

The supplied citation associated with a claimed stem-cell network meta-analysis has no captured source artifact. Its identity and findings therefore cannot be assessed from these inputs. That limitation leaves the stem-cell assertion unverified; it is not evidence that the cited result is false.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review assessed complete extracted article text for the Armstrong and Tian reviews and relied on extracted prose and tables, without inspection of figure graphics or supplements. No bounded freshness search record was supplied. The dated findings remain informative, but these materials do not establish the worldwide absence of a durable regenerative treatment as of November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct a randomized trial in persistent diabetic foot ulcers with documented adequate perfusion, effective offloading and controlled infection, comparing the intervention plus appropriate care with a suitable control receiving appropriate care. Power the study for complete closure and recurrence at one and three years, with amputation as a secondary outcome. These are proposed trial features, grounded in the distinction between initial healing and durability, rather than an established completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized trial evaluates closure and one- and three-year recurrence

completion_criteria.text: Proposed endpoint design: distinguish breakdown at the treated site from new ulcers elsewhere and report both wound-level durability and patient-level ulcer burden. Document loading, protective footwear and continued preventive care throughout follow-up. Account explicitly for death and amputation, which can prevent later recurrence from being observed. Demonstrate that the benefit persists after the study product stops; continued ordinary preventive care should be recorded rather than confused with continued product dependence.
completion_criteria.label: Treated-site durability persists after the study product stops

completion_criteria.text: Proposed success benchmark: require closure and treated-site durability approaching a prespecified, appropriately matched acute traumatic-wound benchmark. The comparator population, matching variables, numerical margins and handling of different mechanical exposures remain to be defined. A higher 12-week healing rate with unchanged recurrence would not satisfy the durable-repair criterion. Claims of regeneration, load-bearing strength or infection resistance would additionally require direct structural and functional measurements.
completion_criteria.label: Closure and treated-site durability approach a matched acute traumatic-wound benchmark

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements: reproduce clinically meaningful benefits across independent centers and clearly described patient groups, with follow-up sufficient to assess the proposed durability endpoints. Report eligibility, adherence, adverse outcomes and practical delivery requirements so the result can be interpreted outside the initial trial. Finite trials would establish the breadth actually demonstrated, not universal effectiveness. Extension to persistently ischemic limbs, unrelieved pressure or other chronic-wound causes would require separate evidence addressing those conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Independent centers reproduce clinically meaningful benefits across defined patient groups

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: DER-01, Clinical restoration of a complete human skin organ, overlaps with the ambition to restore functional skin, but is broader than durable closure of a defined diabetic ulcer. DER-09 could demonstrate valuable local repair without establishing restoration of a complete skin organ. DER-10, In situ reversal of established keloids and pathological cutaneous scars, also concerns the quality of tissue repair, but targets established pathological scarring rather than persistent ulcer closure. Success on either endpoint would not establish success on the other.

Roster-based synthesis: DER-02, One-time genomic cure of severe monogenic skin disease through the epidermal stem-cell compartment, shares an interest in durable benefit but targets a genetic cause and a specified cellular compartment; DER-09 does not require genomic correction or a one-time delivery mechanism. DER-08, Reconstitution of melanocyte stem cells where the follicular reservoir is gone, concerns restoration of a particular cell population. It shares a regenerative theme, while addressing a different tissue function and endpoint.

Roster-based synthesis: DER-03, Antigen-selective erasure of pathogenic cutaneous immune memory, and DER-07, A skin-origin intervention that prevents atopic dermatitis and the atopic march, address immune disease mechanisms and prevention. They overlap with DER-09 only at the broad level of changing persistent skin dysfunction. Neither immune-memory erasure nor prevention of the atopic march establishes durable diabetic wound repair, and DER-09 does not claim those capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: DER-04, Programmable passage of macromolecules and gene editors across intact stratum corneum, could provide a delivery capability for some skin interventions, but crossing intact skin is distinct from repairing an open ulcer and is not a necessary feature of DER-09. DER-05, Epidermal DNA repair sufficient to prevent ultraviolet-driven skin cancer, and DER-06, Therapeutic reset of the mutant epidermal field, concern cancer prevention and altered epidermal cell populations. Their preventive and molecular endpoints remain distinct from ulcer closure, tissue durability and recurrence.

change_log.change: Preserved DER-09's identity and durable-repair ambition while framing regeneration, mechanical strength and infection resistance as proposed capabilities.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence establishes impaired healing and clinical need, but closure and recurrence outcomes alone do not demonstrate these broader biological properties.

change_log.change: Replaced the description of historical healing rates as a therapeutic ceiling with dated population estimates, and retained the supported 12-month nonhealing and three-year recurrence figures.
change_log.reason: The estimates come from different datasets and cannot define a fixed limit on treatment performance.

change_log.change: Separated treated-site breakdown from new ulcers elsewhere and incorporated the reported cohort's 17% identical-site and 48% contralateral-foot recurrence figures.
change_log.reason: Patient-level recurrence cannot be attributed entirely to failure of repaired tissue.

change_log.change: Separated supported treatment findings by source and date: placenta-derived products and negative-pressure therapy in the 2023 review, and EGF, PDGF and PRP in the 2025 analysis.
change_log.reason: The original statement overstated the verified scope of the supplied 2025 network-meta-analysis evidence.

change_log.change: Qualified the stem-cell assertion and removed the inference that newer treatments leave five-year recurrence unchanged at 65%.
change_log.reason: The stem-cell citation lacks a captured artifact, and the verified 2025 analysis does not assess long-term recurrence.

change_log.change: Distinguished direct durable closure from possible reductions in amputation and from unestablished mortality benefit.
change_log.reason: Disease-burden associations do not establish an intervention's effect size, eligible population or survival effect.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to address recurrence location, preventive care, competing outcomes, product withdrawal, direct functional measurements and independent reproduction.
change_log.reason: These distinctions make the proposed clinical and regenerative claims interpretable without presenting candidate thresholds as established standards.

change_log.change: Preserved source-access, extraction and freshness limitations and avoided declaring the capability globally unmet in November 2026.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports dated findings but contains neither a captured stem-cell source nor a bounded search establishing present-day field completeness.

change_log.change: Added explicit overlap and distinctions for every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: The related concepts share selected mechanisms or goals but retain separate identities and completion endpoints.

unresolved_issues: Whether any treatment meets the full durable regenerative specification as of November 1, 2026 remains unresolved; no bounded freshness search record was supplied.
The identity, methods and findings of the source linked through PMID 40821981 remain unverified because no artifact was captured.

The supplied evidence does not determine which residual repair mechanisms must be corrected or how much subsequent ulceration reflects local tissue failure versus renewed injury and disease elsewhere.
The acute traumatic-wound comparator, matching variables, numerical success margins and direct measures of regeneration, strength and infection resistance remain to be specified.
The eligible population, practical treatment requirements and magnitude of any amputation or mortality benefit remain undetermined.
The review's conclusions do not incorporate uninspected figure graphics or supplements; their bearing on the interpretation is unknown.

brief.title: Lasting repair of diabetic foot wounds
possible: People with diabetes could have a stubborn foot wound heal and stay intact after treatment ends. This would apply once poor blood supply, harmful pressure and infection have been addressed, allowing the repaired skin to withstand ordinary activity with protective footwear.
why: Foot ulcers, or open wounds, can limit movement and lead to infection and limb loss. Lasting repair would end persistent wounds for people whose feet remain unhealed despite appropriate care.

sources.who: David G Armstrong, Tze-Woei Tan, Andrew J M Boulton and Sicco A Bus
sources.showed: Their review describes the burden of diabetic foot wounds, treatments that help healing, and the frequent return of ulcers after closure.
sources.quote: These ulcers are associated with impaired physical function, reduced quality of life, and increased health care utilization.
sources.cited_for: The need for lasting repair beyond initial wound closure.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish a treatment that restores functional tissue and keeps the treated wound intact after treatment ends.

sources.showed: Their combined analysis of trials found improved healing with growth factors, proteins involved in tissue repair, and platelet-rich plasma, a concentrated blood preparation.
sources.quote: epidermal growth factor (EGF), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) significantly improved the healing rate.
sources.cited_for: Some treatments improve initial healing beyond standard care.
sources.not_established: Generally weak study methods and no long-term recurrence outcomes leave lasting tissue repair unproven.

shown: Tian and colleagues found that some treatments improved wound healing. Armstrong and colleagues described useful existing care, including pressure relief and infection treatment. Neither review establishes lasting repair after the treatment product stops.
missing: A treatment has yet to demonstrate reliable, lasting closure in wounds that persist despite adequate blood supply, pressure relief and infection control.
Repaired tissue must remain intact after treatment stops and ordinary protected activity resumes.
Restoration of tissue structure, strength under weight and resistance to infection need direct measurement.
Studies must distinguish reopening of the treated wound from new ulcers elsewhere.

milestones.label: A randomized trial establishes closure and lasting benefit
milestones.explanation: A trial assigning treatments by chance would have to compare closure and ulcer return through three years, with underlying foot problems managed. This would test benefit beyond appropriate care.

milestones.label: The treated wound stays closed after treatment ends
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would have to separate reopening from new ulcers, track protection and activity, and account for death and amputation. This would distinguish lasting repair from continued treatment dependence.

milestones.label: Repair approaches healing after a comparable accidental injury
milestones.explanation: Closure and durability would have to approach a suitably matched accidental-wound benchmark, with direct tests of claimed tissue restoration, strength and infection resistance. This would assess repair beyond visible closure.

milestones.label: Independent centers reproduce benefits in defined patient groups
milestones.explanation: Independent centers would have to reproduce meaningful, lasting benefits in clearly described groups and report harms and delivery needs. This would establish how broadly the treatment works in practice.

uncertain: Which remaining barriers to healing must treatment correct, and how much later ulceration reflects tissue failure rather than renewed injury?
What makes an accidental wound a fair comparison, and how close must healing outcomes be?
How many people would qualify, and how much would lasting repair reduce amputations?

page.title: Skin regeneration in diabetic foot ulcers
page.definition: A treatment restores skin structure and function in diabetic foot ulcers that persist after adequate blood supply, pressure relief and infection control. The repaired sites remain closed after treatment ends during protected weight bearing.

goal.need: The goal is to repair ulcers that persist despite standard care and prevent reopening of the repaired site. Diabetic foot ulcers precede about 80% of lower-extremity amputations in people with diabetes. Population recurrence estimates also include ulcers at new sites, so they cannot directly measure failure of the original repair.

completion.title: A treatment regenerates skin and reduces ulcer reopening after treatment withdrawal.
completion.criterion: An adjunct treatment, compared with the same standard care, produces a clinically and statistically significant improvement in complete closure and a reduction in reopening at the treated site after product withdrawal. Closure requires renewed epithelium without drainage or dressings, confirmed 2 weeks apart; follow patients for at least 3 months after closure under protected loading. Histology and direct barrier and mechanical testing demonstrate restoration of skin structure and function. Eligible ulcers persist after adequate perfusion, pressure relief and infection control.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional synthesis; no outside body identified a combined completion test.
completion.basis: Searched FDA's 2006 wound guidance, the 2023 IWGDF guideline, DFCon consensus and NIDDK DFC documents; none defined a combined regeneration-and-withdrawal-durability test or numerical functional threshold. The Atlas uses this provisional combined demonstration without an invented effect-size cutoff. In a 418-person DFC observational study, 21.5% had recurrence by 16 weeks; impaired barrier function predicted recurrence.

milestones.title: A treatment improves epithelial repair in diabetic animal wounds at P < 0.05.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate improved re-epithelialization relative to vehicle in a diabetic-animal wound model, using a controlled comparison with P < 0.05. FDA recognizes animal proof of concept but sets no required percentage or duration. Sun et al. (2023) used 6-mm hind-foot wounds in rats; histology at days 7 and 13 showed greater epithelial repair with RL-QN15. Figure 3 reports n=9 for histological measurements; the starting animal cohort was 80. This establishes preclinical repair activity.
milestones.set_by: Controlled preclinical wound-healing convention, illustrated by Sun et al. (2023); FDA guidance Section III.A recognizes animal proof-of-concept testing. The significance cutoff is experimental, not a regulatory qualification.

milestones.title: At least 7 of 18 patients achieve at least 30% ulcer-area reduction at week 12.
milestones.criterion: Meet the non-futility boundary of NCT03267784: more than 6 of the first 18 treated patients achieve at least 30% wound-area reduction at week 12. The protocol also allowed stopping at 14 or more responders. This phase I/IIa study enrolled adults with type 2 diabetes and neuropathic plantar ulcers after at least 6 weeks of standard care; significant arterial disease and treatment-requiring infection were excluded, and offloading continued. The interim result was 12/18 responders. Recruitment ended early with 23 treated patients; 6/23 achieved complete closure during 12-week efficacy follow-up.
milestones.set_by: NCT03267784 investigators, published Simon two-stage design for topical ABCB5-positive mesenchymal stromal cells; this is a study-specific early clinical threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: This enabled the option to terminate the trial if ≤ 6 or ≥ 14 of the first 18 treated patients were responders.

milestones.title: An adjunct treatment increases complete diabetic foot ulcer closure in a controlled trial.
milestones.criterion: Show a clinically and statistically significant increase versus control in complete closure: renewed epithelium, no drainage or dressing need, confirmed 2 weeks apart. Omnigraft's 307-person study found closure within 16 weeks in 79/154 versus 49/153 patients (P=0.0007). Tian's 51-trial synthesis (3,401 participants) and Hu's 99-trial synthesis (7,356 participants) report healing benefits without establishing regeneration. On 15 September 2026, PolarityBio reported that the 120-person COVER DFUS II study met its 12-week closure endpoint; this sponsor report was not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Chronic Cutaneous Ulcer and Burn Wounds—Developing Products for Treatment, Section IV.G.1.a; nonbinding guidance.
milestones.threshold_quote: clinically and statistically significant greater proportion of subjects

milestones.title: A treated diabetic foot ulcer remains completely closed for at least three months.
milestones.criterion: Sustain complete closure through at least 3 months after closure. FDA recommends this observation interval to distinguish healing from transient coverage; it specifies no minimum proportion remaining healed. The Omnigraft study added three monthly visits after its 16-week treatment phase. Recurrence occurred in 15/79 healed Omnigraft patients and 13/49 healed controls; the difference was not statistically significant. Only 106/154 and 82/153 randomized patients, respectively, completed the study through follow-up. These data do not establish reduced recurrence.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Section IV.G.1.a: the published criterion specifies the follow-up interval and purpose, not a universal product-level recurrence cutoff.
milestones.threshold_quote: at least 3 months following complete wound closure

not_found: Full text for PMID 40821981 could not be read at PMC or PeerJ; its identity and abstract were verified in PubMed.
ClinicalTrials.gov did not expose a readable detailed record for NCT06140303.
No retrieved controlled human study demonstrated the combined regeneration and post-withdrawal recurrence benefit.

results.finding: In a 3,401-patient meta-analysis, EGF increased the healing rate versus standard care (RR 1.55).
results.detail: The analysis included 51 randomized trials, but the text does not establish that healing met the required complete-closure definition or was confirmed two weeks apart. The sample size is for the full analysis, not necessarily the EGF comparison.
results.quote: Compared to SOC, EGF (RR = 1.55, 95% CI = 1.26–1.96), PDGF (RR = 1.29, 95% CI = 1.06–1.60), and PRP (RR = 1.24, 95% CI = 1.07–1.50) significantly improved the healing rate, with statistically significant differences.

results.finding: RL-QN15 improved re-epithelialization in diabetic rat wounds; histology n=9.
results.detail: The vehicle-controlled experiment showed greater epithelial repair on day 7. Figure 3’s legend reports P < 0.005, but the supplied text does not identify which comparisons carry that significance; the figure itself is not shown.
results.quote: In the RL-QN15-treated group, however, re-epithelialization and granulation tissue regeneration were observed on day 7, and collagen deposition and VEGFB expression started to appear.

results.finding: In NCT03267784, 12 of the first 18 treated patients achieved at least 30% wound-area reduction at week 12.
results.detail: The interim result exceeded the non-futility boundary of more than 6 responders. Recruitment continued but ended early after 23 patients were treated.
results.quote: As in an interim analysis 12 of 18 patients emerged as responders, recruitment was continued.

results.finding: Omnigraft trial (307 participants): complete closure occurred in 51.3% versus 32.0% of controls within 16 weeks.
results.detail: The difference was statistically significant (p=0.0007). The FDA summary does not specify that closure required renewed epithelium, no drainage or dressing, or confirmation two weeks apart.

results.finding: In 255 patients, fish skin graft increased 16-week closure by 17.6 percentage points versus standard care.
results.detail: Closure was defined as reepithelialization without drainage or need for dressing and confirmed 14 days later. The trial included some ischemic or infected wounds and did not establish skin regeneration.

results.finding: ON101 trial (236 patients): complete closure occurred in 60.7% versus 35.1% with absorbent dressing.
results.detail: The 25.6-percentage-point difference was statistically significant (P < .001). Healing required epithelialization without drainage or dressings at two consecutive visits, scheduled two weeks apart. Some patients with plantar ulcers did not use recommended off-loading devices.
results.quote: Seventy-four patients (60.7%) in the ON101 group vs 40 (35.1%) in the comparator group achieved ulcer closure within 16 weeks

results.finding: ODINN IFSG vs SOC (262 DFU patients): mean 12-week wound area reduction 62.53% vs 30.82% (p=0.007); no ≥30% responder count reported.

results.finding: ODINN RCT (262 DFU patients): IFSG increased 16-week complete closure vs SOC, 40.6% (54/133) vs 23.3% (30/129), p=0.003.
results.detail: Deep UT grade 2/3 DFUs; ITT analysis; closure adjudicated by blinded committee. Significant complete closure increase in controlled trial.

results.detail: 24-week healed proportion is cumulative closure at a timepoint, not confirmation that ulcers remained closed for ≥3 months after initial closure; no recurrence data.

results.finding: TWO2 increased complete DFU closure at 12 weeks: 15/36 (41.7%) vs 5/37 (13.5%), P=0.007.
results.detail: Double-blind, sham-controlled RCT in 73 randomized patients; complete epithelialization confirmed at a second visit 2 weeks later; enrollment stopped early at first planned analysis.
results.quote: In the active arm 15 wounds (41.7%) completely healed versus 5 wounds (13.5%) in the sham arm at 12 weeks [Pearsonx2 5 7.27 (1 df), P 5 0.007].

results.finding: At 12 months, only 1/15 (6.7%) TWO2-healed DFUs recurred; sham recurrence was 2/5 (40%, P=0.070).
results.detail: Follow-up to 12 months postenrollment exceeds 3 months after 12-week closure; recurrence reduction vs sham was not statistically significant, but m4 sets no minimum proportion remaining healed.
results.quote: At 12 months postenrollment, only 1 of 15 healed ulcers (6.7%) in the active arm recurred, compared with 2 of 5 healed ulcers (40%) in the sham arm, falling just short of statistical significance (P 5 0.070).
